subtopics.title: Origins and evolution
subtopics.summary: The SCO grew out of the Shanghai Five, created in 1996 by China, Russia and three Central Asian states to address border issues and build military confidence. Uzbekistan joined in 2001, leading to the SCO's establishment on 15 June 2001 in Shanghai. The SCO Charter was signed in 2002 and entered into force in 2003. Membership later widened, with India and Pakistan becoming full members in 2017, Iran in 2023 and Belarus in 2024.

subtopics.title: Institutions and membership
subtopics.summary: The SCO is a Permanent Eurasian Inter-Governmental Organisation that links Central Asia, South Asia, China, Russia and Iran. It has 10 member states and 2 observers, with headquarters in Beijing. Its Council of Heads of State is the highest decision-making body, while the Council of Heads of Government handles economic and developmental cooperation. Counter-terrorism cooperation is run by the Regional Anti-Terrorist Structure based in Tashkent.

Council of Heads of Government: economic and developmental cooperation

Focus areas: regional security, counter-terrorism, economic and connectivity cooperation
Also covers political dialogue and cultural and people-to-people exchanges

subtopics.title: Key outcomes of the 26th Summit
subtopics.summary: The 26th SCO Summit was held from 31 August to 1 September 2026 in Bishkek, Kyrgyzstan, marking the organisation's 25th anniversary under the chairmanship of President Sadyr Japarov. Leaders adopted the Bishkek Declaration as the summit's principal political document and approved 28 outcome documents. Kyrgyzstan transferred the SCO Presidency to Pakistan for 2026-27, and English was added as an official and working language.

subtopics.title: India and the SCO
subtopics.summary: India frames its SCO engagement around three pillars: Security, Connectivity and Opportunity for regional cooperation. The SCO gives India institutional access to Central Asia, bypassing the lack of direct overland routes, and supports long-term energy and resource security. Frictions include the China-Pakistan strategic axis, India's refusal of the BRI because CPEC passes through disputed territories, and slow progress on payment arrangements and transport corridors. India also took part in the 6th World Nomad Games 2026 with its largest-ever contingent of 87 members.

quizzes.passage: The Shanghai Cooperation Organisation has grown from a regional grouping into a wide Eurasian platform that links Central Asia, South Asia, China, Russia and Iran. Its work covers regional security, counter-terrorism, economic and connectivity cooperation, political dialogue, and cultural and people-to-people exchanges. Its leaders meet every year, and the host state rotates along with the chairmanship. The latest summit was held in Bishkek, the capital of Kyrgyzstan, and was chaired by the country's president. The gathering marked the organisation's 25th anniversary, and its theme focused on sustainable peace, development and prosperity. Leaders reviewed a large set of outcome documents on security, economy, energy, climate, institutional development and culture. The summit also reaffirmed the need for collective action against terrorism and adopted the main political document of the meeting. The summit also dealt with new mechanisms against drug trafficking and the financing of extremism, which the organisation treats as shared regional threats. A standing regional structure for counter-terrorism frames terror financing and radicalisation as collective concerns. The agenda also includes transport corridors and payment arrangements. Such a summit shows how the SCO tries to balance security concerns with its economic goals, while giving member states a common forum for their policies. It is a useful window into the organisation's priorities.

quizzes.passage: The organisation's story begins with a grouping built to settle old disputes. Its early members were mainly concerned with borders between neighbours and with building trust among their armed forces. Over time, the group admitted new members and widened its agenda from border questions to security, trade and people-to-people contact. Membership has grown in stages, and some countries first took part as observers before becoming full members. Today the organisation has a secretariat that handles routine administration, and a council of heads of state that takes the most important decisions. Its counter-terrorism work runs through a regional structure based in Uzbekistan. The chairmanship moves between member states each year, which keeps the organisation's leadership spread across the region. Its leaders also meet at the annual summit, where the chair passes from one member to the next. The organisation's objectives include strengthening mutual trust, good-neighbourliness and mutual support on security and counter-terrorism. It also aims to promote cooperation in trade, economy, connectivity, transport, digital economy and environmental protection. Over the years, members have built a shared set of institutions, and their common work is coordinated through the secretariat and the heads of state council. The Shanghai Cooperation Organisation describes its goals as peace, security, stability, economic cooperation and cultural exchange in the SCO region.
